title: Reduced and verbless clauses: while waiting, when in doubt
tagline: Keep the conjunction, drop the subject and 'be': a time, reason or concession clause shrinks to a few words.
exam: Reading & Use of English Part 4 — key word transformations
Reading & Use of English Part 2 — open cloze: while, once, though, if before a reduced clause
Writing Part 2 — report, review or proposal: compact, formal style
Writing Part 1 — essay: concise concession (Though small, …)
why: Advanced writers keep the conjunction and cut the rest: While waiting for the bus instead of While I was waiting for the bus, or If necessary instead of If it is necessary. This is how reports, reviews and instructions sound at C1, and Part 2 open cloze often removes the conjunction itself. The price is one strict rule: the missing subject is always the subject of the main clause, so a mismatch makes a dangling modifier.

diagrams.title: From full clause to reduced clause

before.text: While Sofia was waiting for her results, she revised the vocabulary again.

after.text: While waiting for her results, Sofia revised the vocabulary again.

steps: Check that the subject of both clauses is the same person or thing (Sofia).
Keep the conjunction (While) and delete the subject and the auxiliary was.
Use the -ing form: While waiting — the conjunction stays in the sentence to show the relationship.

rows.label: Pattern
cells: the main subject differs from the hidden one

rows.label: Example
cells: While waiting for the bus, Liam read a book.
While waiting for the bus, the rain started.

rows.label: Problem
cells: none: Liam waited and Liam read
the rain cannot be the one waiting

rows.label: Fix
cells: While we were waiting for the bus, the rain started.

rows: While I was crossing the road, I saw Nadia.
While crossing the road, I saw Nadia.
Before she leaves, she checks the windows.
Before leaving, she checks the windows.

use.point: Time clauses: while, after, before, on, since, once + -ing

examples.text: While waiting for the interview, Mateo reread his notes.
After finishing the experiment, the students cleaned the lab.
examples.note: = after they had finished; one action follows another

examples.text: Sofia always checks her bag before leaving the classroom.
examples.note: = before she leaves; the reduced clause can come second

examples.text: Not knowing what to say, Liam stayed silent.
examples.note: = because he did not know; negative placed before the -ing

examples.text: Being new to the school, Nadia asked for a map.
examples.note: being = because she was; the conjunction is dropped

examples.text: Unable to find a seat, we sat on the steps.

use.point: Verbless clauses: conjunction + adjective, noun or preposition

examples.text: When in doubt, ask your teacher before you submit.
examples.note: = when you are in doubt; a set phrase

examples.text: Though tired, Liam refused to stop until the last page was done.
Once inside, the visitors were handed a map.
examples.note: once they were inside: visitors is the subject

examples.text: Although a keen reader, Mateo had never finished a long novel.
examples.note: Mateo = a keen reader: subject and noun phrase match

watch_out.wrong: While waiting for the bus, the rain started.
watch_out.right: While we were waiting for the bus, the rain started.
watch_out.why: Dangling modifier: the rain cannot be the one waiting.

watch_out.wrong: After to finish the report, she emailed it.
watch_out.right: After finishing the report, she emailed it.
watch_out.why: After a conjunction or preposition use the -ing form, not the to-infinitive.

watch_out.wrong: Before to leave, check the windows.
Because tired, Mateo went to bed early.
watch_out.right: Being tired (or Because he was tired), Mateo went to bed early.
watch_out.why: Because cannot introduce a verbless clause; use being or a full clause.

watch_out.wrong: Although tired, the exam seemed endless.
watch_out.right: Although he was tired, the exam seemed endless.
watch_out.why: The exam is not tired: either add a subject or change the main clause so that it names the tired person.

watch_out.wrong: Knowing not what to do, Nadia asked for help.
watch_out.right: Not knowing what to do, Nadia asked for help.
watch_out.why: In modern English the negative not comes before the -ing form.

dialogue.title: Tightening the lab report
dialogue.context: Miss Vega is helping Sofia, Mateo and Nadia shorten their lab reports before the deadline.

lines.speaker: Miss Vega
lines.text: Your report is clear, but it's wordy. If necessary, cut each sentence by a third.

lines.speaker: Sofia
lines.text: I wrote 'While we were waiting for the results, we cleaned the equipment'. Should it be While waiting for the results, we cleaned the equipment?

lines.speaker: Miss Vega
lines.text: Yes. The subject is the same, so you can reduce it.

lines.speaker: Mateo
lines.text: What about 'Because I did not know the exact amount, I used the larger flask'?

lines.speaker: Miss Vega
lines.text: Not knowing the exact amount, I used the larger flask. Much tighter.

lines.speaker: Nadia
lines.text: Though tired, we repeated the test twice. Is that acceptable in a report?

lines.speaker: Miss Vega
lines.text: It's fine, but keep the tone formal. When in doubt, use the full clause.

lines.speaker: Sofia
lines.text: I also have 'After we had finished, we weighed the sample.' Can I write After finishing, we weighed the sample?

lines.speaker: Miss Vega
lines.text: Perfect. Just check that once inside the lab, the reader knows who is doing what.

lines.speaker: Mateo
lines.text: Understood. Before submitting it, I'll read every reduced clause for a hidden subject.

items.sentence: ___ for the bus, Liam realised he had left his wallet at home.
After ___ the form, hand it to the receptionist.
Sofia always checks her work before ___ it in.
When ___, ask Miss Vega before you start.
items.why: verbless set phrase: when in doubt

items.sentence: ___ tired, Nadia stayed to help clear up.
items.why: though + adjective is a concession; despite and because do not take it

items.sentence: Please submit the form online or, ___, in person.
___ the exam, the students were told to stay seated.
items.why: after + -ing; the hidden subject (the students) matches the main clause

practice.instructions: Complete each sentence with one word or the correct form of the word in brackets.

items.sentence: While ___ (cross) the road, always look both ways.
___ (not/know) which train to take, Sofia asked a guard.
Before ___ (leave) the lab, make sure the equipment is switched off.
___ necessary, you can retake the test in January.
Once ___ the building, visitors must sign in at reception.
After ___ (speak) to the head, the parents felt reassured.
___ (be) unsure of the date, I checked the calendar again.

practice.instructions: Complete the second sentence so that it has a similar meaning to the first, using the word given. Do not change the word given. Use between two and five words.

items.first: While I was waiting for the doctor, I read a magazine.
items.second_end: for the doctor, I read a magazine.

items.first: Because he didn't know the way, Mateo took a taxi.
items.second_end: the way, Mateo took a taxi.

items.first: After she finished her homework, Sofia went online.
If it is necessary, you can ring me after ten.
items.second_end: , you can ring me after ten.

Before she left the office, Nadia locked the drawers.
items.second_end: the office, Nadia locked the drawers.

summary: Keep the conjunction (while, after, before, once, though, if, when) and drop the subject and be: While waiting …, If necessary ….
A reduced clause may contain -ing, an adjective, a noun phrase or a prepositional phrase: Though tired, When in doubt, Once inside.
Reason clauses lose the conjunction altogether: Not knowing what to do, …; put not before the -ing form.
The hidden subject must be the subject of the main clause; otherwise you have a dangling modifier.
After a conjunction or preposition use -ing, never the to-infinitive: after finishing, before leaving.
